# Making changes to Claudinite without hurting consumers

> **Status: provisional — beliefs, not law.** Every entry here says what we're *currently* doing
> and *why we think* it helps. When an entry blocks a better change, challenge the entry rather
> than contorting the change; being cited in this guide is not, by itself, a reason something
> must stay. We'll solidify entries once they've earned it.

Claudinite is vendored into every consuming repo, so a change here lands in many places, on the
fleet's schedule, usually with no human watching. This guide collects what we currently believe
about making such changes safely. It is a maintainer document for sessions working *in* this
repo; it is not part of the vendored corpus.

## First, know which channel the change travels

Since the fleet moved to the tracked vendored mount (vendoring/DESIGN.md, phases 1–3 complete),
the channel model is small — nothing reaches a consumer instantly, and nothing arrives outside
its git history:

- **The vendored corpus** (`engine/`, `packs/` — checks, prose, bundled skills) — each member
  holds a tracked snapshot under `.claudinite/shared/`, converged **whole-set** to the canon
  head by the nightly refresh and stamped with its provenance. Propagation lags one nightly,
  lands as a reviewable commit on the member's `claudinite/maintenance` PR (auto-merged on
  `auto-merge` delivery once the repo's checks pass, held for the owner on `review`), and the
  rollback story is the same channel: fix the canon, the next nightly re-heals. A wrong
  *blocking* check still fails every member's Stop hook — visible and recoverable, but
  fleet-wide noise, so treat check changes as production changes.
- **Migration notes** (`engine/migrations/<date>-<slug>/`, or `packs/<pack>/migrations/<date>-<slug>/`) — the channel for anything convergence
  can't express: renames of consumer-held wiring, declaration rewrites, one-off agentic steps.
  Stamp-day-gated and idempotent; the note's `legacyPresent` telemetry says when the fleet has
  moved and (for `retire: 'auto'`) retires the record itself.
- **Copied artifacts** (pack `stubs/`, seeded configs) — these do **not** propagate at all. Each
  consumer holds its own copy, which drifts silently unless a check enforces its shape. Changing
  the source file alone only affects repos bootstrapped *after* the change.
- **Bootstrap wiring** (the committed artifacts [bootstrap.md](bootstrap.md) seeds:
  `settings.json` hook registrations, the two gitignore lines, the pack declaration) —
  propagates through the nightly update's idempotent backfills on the same delivery PR.
  The discipline: a change here is written as steps that **converge from every layout in the
  wild**, not just from the latest.

Out-of-repo state remains the one channel git never reaches: a web environment's pasted Setup
script is snapshotted at environment build. A change that moves what the pasted script calls
needs the script's own probe to fail fast and a member issue asking for the one human action
(re-paste).

## Migrating a copied artifact (stubs and the like)

Because copies won't move on their own, we currently migrate them through the conformance
checks, in one Claudinite-only change:

1. Change the source artifact in the pack (the stub under `packs/<pack>/stubs/`).
2. Make sure the pack's conformance check enforces the properties that changed, with a `fix`
   that says how to align (usually "re-copy the stub"). A consumer's own next session then
   raises a blocking finding and performs the migration in that repo — no per-repo PR from
   here.
3. Keep the pack's `detect` fingerprint **tolerant of the legacy shape** while copies migrate
   (e.g. a `LEGACY_*` list beside the current constant), so a fresh `--init` still recognizes a
   not-yet-migrated repo and seeds the pack.

Fleet-wide "everyone has migrated" telemetry exists — declare the rename as a
[baseline migration](engine/migrations/README.md), **in the same change that introduces the tolerance**: a

{"number":1693,"title":"Promote three member packs onto the canon shelf","body":"Closes #1692

CrosswordChat and LaughCounter each grew a local pack beside a canon pack they had never declared, so the same rules were being maintained twice. This lands the residue where the canon already owns the territory, and opens one new pack for the facet nothing covered.

## `packs/web-speech` — widened

Six API-contract checks and two rules, from CrosswordChat's `local/browser-speech`.

The rules canon already carried are untouched: the screen-capture constraint trap, the 1.2 s / 1.8 s endpoint window, the biasing gate, the error taxonomy, the lazy voice list, the `chrome.tts` relay. What is new:

- **Interim results are a signal, not input.** They arrive on the *same* `result` event as the finished utterance and are revised several times per utterance, so a handler that delivers `results[i][0].transcript` acts on words the user had not finished saying — and acts again on each revision.
- **The echo guard belongs in the application, not at the capture layer.** Chrome's automatic echo cancellation is a loopback of *page* playout: it attenuates `speechSynthesis` and never sees `chrome.tts`, whose audio the OS renders. That residual echo cannot be reached by any capture constraint, which is why matching the transcript against what you just spoke is the design rather than a stopgap — and why reaching for `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` means the guard that would have worked never gets written.

Two existing rules each take one clause: run the mic preflight even when permission is already granted (otherwise the device is warmed only on the first grant), and treat voice order and speaking rate as user-facing settings rather than constants.

The six checks are pack-level rather than skill-bundled, since they judge the API contracts themselves rather than where the code runs. All six parse the call site rather than grepping for a name, comments stripped first — so a wrapper that delegates its terminal handling, a constraints object hoisted into a constant, and a switch that dispatches side effects rather than mapping a value all stay quiet. What unites them is that their breach is **silent**: nothing throws, nothing logs, and the app keeps showing a live session while the user is heard by nobody.

## `packs/macos` — widened

`swift-toolchain-gate` only. The pack's prose already carried the rule — `/usr/bin/swift` is a stub present on every Mac that pops an 8 GB install prompt rather than failing, so `command -v swift` must sit behind `xcode-select -p`. The check was the missing half.

LaughCounter's other two local checks do not come across: they are hardcoded to `mac/Sources/` and `AudioHub.swift`, and canon already holds generalized equivalents in `signal-teardown-routing` and `sudden-termination-vs-teardown`. `references.md` is created here on its first entry.

## `packs/host-page` — new

Being a guest in a web app you do not own. `web-scraping` acquires a site's data from outside it, `chrome-extension` covers how your code reaches the page, `headless-browser` drives a browser you own — none covers what to do once you are inside somebody else's page.

Eleven rules, generalized off CrosswordChat's `local/host-page-adaptation` with its evidence citations stripped (the `xwd__` token, `page-adapter/`, the REQ ids, the fixture paths). Three checks, sharing one failure mode: an observer that outlives its feature, a synthetic event that does not bubble, and one aimed outside the app root all leave `dispatchEvent` returning true and the page simply not responding — indistinguishable from "the app rejects untrusted events", which is the wrong conclusion and an expensive one to back out of.

Declared by hand. There is no honest fingerprint: a content script, a `dispatchEvent` and a `MutationObserver` are equally the shapes of code running on its *own* page, so a marker that cannot tell a guest from a host would suspect the pack in every DOM repo in the fleet.

## Folders touched

```
packs/web-speech/     6 checks + shared call-site helpers, 2 rules and 2 clauses,
                      references entries for all six, rule index and checks table
packs/macos/          swift-toolchain-gate + its test, references.md created
packs/host-page/      new pack: manifest, 11 rules, 3 checks, README index,
                      references, badge, VERSIONS
packs/                directory.GENERATED.md regenerated for the new pack
```

## Verification

Full canon suite, `node --test` over the CI test roots: **3,214 of 3,217 pass**. All nine new checks are covered both ways — firing on a violating source and silent on the legitimate spellings that a text scan would false-alarm on.

Three failures, none from this diff:

- `packs/claudinite-growth/VERSIONS.md` claims `60903.5` on two rows (lines 10 and 44), failing `pack-version-claimed-once`. Pre-existing on `main` — `git show origin/main:packs/claudinite-growth/VERSIONS.md` shows both rows. Filed as #1694.
- `engine-pack-lane-shims` reports "this checkout is too shallow to walk origin/main's pack history". An artifact of this container's `--depth 1` clone; CI checks out with `fetch-depth: 0`.
- `dev/tools/tests/badges.test.mjs` flagged the new badge as untracked before it was staged; green once committed.

I have not run the canon's own conformance sweep beyond the test suite, so CI is the first full signal on that half.

input.body:
Closes #1692

CrosswordChat and LaughCounter each grew a local pack beside a canon pack they had never declared, so the same rules were being maintained twice. This lands the residue where the canon already owns the territory, and opens one new pack for the facet nothing covered.

## `packs/web-speech` — widened

Six API-contract checks and two rules, from CrosswordChat's `local/browser-speech`.

The rules canon already carried are untouched: the screen-capture constraint trap, the 1.2 s / 1.8 s endpoint window, the biasing gate, the error taxonomy, the lazy voice list, the `chrome.tts` relay. What is new:

- **Interim results are a signal, not input.** They arrive on the *same* `result` event as the finished utterance and are revised several times per utterance, so a handler that delivers `results[i][0].transcript` acts on words the user had not finished saying — and acts again on each revision.
- **The echo guard belongs in the application, not at the capture layer.** Chrome's automatic echo cancellation is a loopback of *page* playout: it attenuates `speechSynthesis` and never sees `chrome.tts`, whose audio the OS renders. That residual echo cannot be reached by any capture constraint, which is why matching the transcript against what you just spoke is the design rather than a stopgap — and why reaching for `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` means the guard that would have worked never gets written.

Two existing rules each take one clause: run the mic preflight even when permission is already granted (otherwise the device is warmed only on the first grant), and treat voice order and speaking rate as user-facing settings rather than constants.

The six checks are pack-level rather than skill-bundled, since they judge the API contracts themselves rather than where the code runs. All six parse the call site rather than grepping for a name, comments stripped first — so a wrapper that delegates its terminal handling, a constraints object hoisted into a constant, and a switch that dispatches side effects rather than mapping a value all stay quiet. What unites them is that their breach is **silent**: nothing throws, nothing logs, and the app keeps showing a live session while the user is heard by nobody.

## `packs/macos` — widened

`swift-toolchain-gate` only. The pack's prose already carried the rule — `/usr/bin/swift` is a stub present on every Mac that pops an 8 GB install prompt rather than failing, so `command -v swift` must sit behind `xcode-select -p`. The check was the missing half.

LaughCounter's other two local checks do not come across: they are hardcoded to `mac/Sources/` and `AudioHub.swift`, and canon already holds generalized equivalents in `signal-teardown-routing` and `sudden-termination-vs-teardown`. `references.md` is created here on its first entry.

## `packs/host-page` — new

Being a guest in a web app you do not own. `web-scraping` acquires a site's data from outside it, `chrome-extension` covers how your code reaches the page, `headless-browser` drives a browser you own — none covers what to do once you are inside somebody else's page.

Eleven rules, generalized off CrosswordChat's `local/host-page-adaptation` with its evidence citations stripped (the `xwd__` token, `page-adapter/`, the REQ ids, the fixture paths). Three checks, sharing one failure mode: an observer that outlives its feature, a synthetic event that does not bubble, and one aimed outside the app root all leave `dispatchEvent` returning true and the page simply not responding — indistinguishable from "the app rejects untrusted events", which is the wrong conclusion and an expensive one to back out of.

Declared by hand. There is no honest fingerprint: a content script, a `dispatchEvent` and a `MutationObserver` are equally the shapes of code running on its *own* page, so a marker that cannot tell a guest from a host would suspect the pack in every DOM repo in the fleet.

## Consumer safety

Nine rules become blocking here, and canon CI cannot see a consumer. **No fleet member declares `web-speech`, `macos` or `host-page`** — checked across all sixteen — so nothing turns red overnight and the change is genuinely additive, which per `consumer-safe-changes.md` makes the rehearsal fixture the honest answer rather than a migration record.

`voice-on-a-host-page` is a new fixture shape: a member declaring `web-speech` and `host-page` over source in the exact shape all nine rules engage on — a recognizer wired for every terminal event, interim results gated on `isFinal`, a total error map, a preflight releasing its tracks in a `finally`, an observer that disconnects, synthetic input that bubbles and targets a node inside the app. It proves the rules inert on a conforming consumer rather than passing by dodging the gates. CrosswordChat is about to become exactly this shape (#396).

`macos-app` gains a diagnostic script for the same reason: `swift-toolchain-gate` scans shell and workflow files, of which that fixture had none, so the rule would have passed there vacuously.

Writing the fixture caught two faults in this PR's own work, which is the point of it: the synthetic keystroke was not using the helper-and-spread idiom `host-page`'s own rule prescribes, and the recognizer lacked the `pagehide` teardown `web-speech` already required.

## Folders touched

```
packs/web-speech/     6 checks + shared call-site helpers, 2 rules and 2 clauses,
                      references entries for all six, rule index and checks table
packs/macos/          swift-toolchain-gate + its test, references.md created
packs/host-page/      new pack: manifest, 11 rules, 3 checks, README index,
                      references, badge, VERSIONS
packs/                directory.GENERATED.md regenerated; README.md catalog entry
vendoring/rehearsal/  the voice-on-a-host-page shape, and a script for macos-app
```

## Verification

All three gates green on the current head:

- Full canon suite over the CI test roots — **3,258 of 3,258 pass**.
- `check_the_work.mjs` (the Stop-hook runner) — **exit 0**.
- `check_the_world.mjs` — **0 blocking**.

Three findings were fixed along the way, two of which only the work-scope runner sees:

- `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` is a *hand-maintained* index, so a new pack does not appear in it by existing on disk. Added, and the `web-speech` / `macos` counts corrected.
- `consumer-safe-change` — resolved with the fixtures above.
- `squash-merge-history` — the branch had picked up a merge commit while resolving a base-branch conflict. Rebased out; the branch is three commits.

The `pack-version-claimed-once` failure this PR originally sat behind was fixed on `main` by #1680 and is closed as #1694.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

{"number":1693,"title":"Promote three member packs onto the canon shelf","body":"Closes #1692

CrosswordChat and LaughCounter each grew a local pack beside a canon pack they had never declared, so the same rules were being maintained twice. This lands the residue where the canon already owns the territory, and opens one new pack for the facet nothing covered.

## `packs/web-speech` — widened

Six API-contract checks and two rules, from CrosswordChat's `local/browser-speech`.

The rules canon already carried are untouched: the screen-capture constraint trap, the 1.2 s / 1.8 s endpoint window, the biasing gate, the error taxonomy, the lazy voice list, the `chrome.tts` relay. What is new:

- **Interim results are a signal, not input.** They arrive on the *same* `result` event as the finished utterance and are revised several times per utterance, so a handler that delivers `results[i][0].transcript` acts on words the user had not finished saying — and acts again on each revision.
- **The echo guard belongs in the application, not at the capture layer.** Chrome's automatic echo cancellation is a loopback of *page* playout: it attenuates `speechSynthesis` and never sees `chrome.tts`, whose audio the OS renders. That residual echo cannot be reached by any capture constraint, which is why matching the transcript against what you just spoke is the design rather than a stopgap — and why reaching for `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` means the guard that would have worked never gets written.

Two existing rules each take one clause: run the mic preflight even when permission is already granted (otherwise the device is warmed only on the first grant), and treat voice order and speaking rate as user-facing settings rather than constants.

The six checks are pack-level rather than skill-bundled, since they judge the API contracts themselves rather than where the code runs. All six parse the call site rather than grepping for a name, comments stripped first — so a wrapper that delegates its terminal handling, a constraints object hoisted into a constant, and a switch that dispatches side effects rather than mapping a value all stay quiet. What unites them is that their breach is **silent**: nothing throws, nothing logs, and the app keeps showing a live session while the user is heard by nobody.

## `packs/macos` — widened

`swift-toolchain-gate` only. The pack's prose already carried the rule — `/usr/bin/swift` is a stub present on every Mac that pops an 8 GB install prompt rather than failing, so `command -v swift` must sit behind `xcode-select -p`. The check was the missing half.

LaughCounter's other two local checks do not come across: they are hardcoded to `mac/Sources/` and `AudioHub.swift`, and canon already holds generalized equivalents in `signal-teardown-routing` and `sudden-termination-vs-teardown`. `references.md` is created here on its first entry.

## `packs/host-page` — new

Being a guest in a web app you do not own. `web-scraping` acquires a site's data from outside it, `chrome-extension` covers how your code reaches the page, `headless-browser` drives a browser you own — none covers what to do once you are inside somebody else's page.

Eleven rules, generalized off CrosswordChat's `local/host-page-adaptation` with its evidence citations stripped (the `xwd__` token, `page-adapter/`, the REQ ids, the fixture paths). Three checks, sharing one failure mode: an observer that outlives its feature, a synthetic event that does not bubble, and one aimed outside the app root all leave `dispatchEvent` returning true and the page simply not responding — indistinguishable from "the app rejects untrusted events", which is the wrong conclusion and an expensive one to back out of.

Declared by hand. There is no honest fingerprint: a content script, a `dispatchEvent` and a `MutationObserver` are equally the shapes of code running on its *own* page, so a marker that cannot tell a guest from a host would suspect the pack in every DOM repo in the fleet.

## Consumer safety

Nine rules become blocking here, and canon CI cannot see a consumer. **No fleet member declares `web-speech`, `macos` or `host-page`** — checked across all sixteen — so nothing turns red overnight and the change is genuinely additive, which per `consumer-safe-changes.md` makes the rehearsal fixture the honest answer rather than a migration record.

`voice-on-a-host-page` is a new fixture shape: a member declaring `web-speech` and `host-page` over source in the exact shape all nine rules engage on — a recognizer wired for every terminal event, interim results gated on `isFinal`, a total error map, a preflight releasing its tracks in a `finally`, an observer that disconnects, synthetic input that bubbles and targets a node inside the app. It proves the rules inert on a conforming consumer rather than passing by dodging the gates. CrosswordChat is about to become exactly this shape (#396).

`macos-app` gains a diagnostic script for the same reason: `swift-toolchain-gate` scans shell and workflow files, of which that fixture had none, so the rule would have passed there vacuously.

Writing the fixture caught two faults in this PR's own work, which is the point of it: the synthetic keystroke was not using the helper-and-spread idiom `host-page`'s own rule prescribes, and the recognizer lacked the `pagehide` teardown `web-speech` already required.

## Folders touched

```
packs/web-speech/     6 checks + shared call-site helpers, 2 rules and 2 clauses,
                      references entries for all six, rule index and checks table
packs/macos/          swift-toolchain-gate + its test, references.md created
packs/host-page/      new pack: manifest, 11 rules, 3 checks, README index,
                      references, badge, VERSIONS
packs/                directory.GENERATED.md regenerated; README.md catalog entry
vendoring/rehearsal/  the voice-on-a-host-page shape, and a script for macos-app
```

## Verification

All three gates green on the current head:

- Full canon suite over the CI test roots — **3,258 of 3,258 pass**.
- `check_the_work.mjs` (the Stop-hook runner) — **exit 0**.
- `check_the_world.mjs` — **0 blocking**.

Three findings were fixed along the way, two of which only the work-scope runner sees:

- `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` is a *hand-maintained* index, so a new pack does not appear in it by existing on disk. Added, and the `web-speech` / `macos` counts corrected.
- `consumer-safe-change` — resolved with the fixtures above.
- `squash-merge-history` — the branch had picked up a merge commit while resolving a base-branch conflict. Rebased out; the branch is three commits.

The `pack-version-claimed-once` failure this PR originally sat behind was fixed on `main` by #1680 and is closed as #1694.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- fleet-triage: Survey every open issue across the whole missingbulb fleet, split the queue items from the plain ones, and attribute each parked task to the cause that actually parked it. Use when asked for a triage run, a fleet overview, a stuck-tasks analysis, or "all open issues across the fleet".
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
